glossary.definition: The share of predictions that match the true labels: (true positives + true negatives) / all examples. It can hide poor minority-class performance on imbalanced data.
A system that observes context, chooses an action, uses tools or an environment, and updates its behavior from feedback toward a goal.
A controlled comparison that removes or changes one component at a time to estimate how much it contributes to the result.
A mechanism that assigns context-dependent weights to information. In self-attention, queries and keys determine how values are combined.
A simple, established, or strong reference method that a proposed approach must be compared against using the same data and protocol.
A subset of training examples used together to compute one estimate of the loss and its gradient.
Error caused by restrictive assumptions that prevent a model from representing the underlying pattern; high bias often appears as underfitting.
Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies. Among examples assigned probability near 0.8, roughly 80% should be positive for a calibrated model.
A dataset in which some labels occur much more often than others. Accuracy may be misleading; inspect per-class precision, recall, F1, and confusion counts.
A table of actual versus predicted labels. For binary classification it contains true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives.
A resampling procedure that repeats train/validation evaluation across folds. Keep a final test set separate when it is needed for a final estimate.
Information from evaluation examples or the future enters training, preprocessing, feature selection, or model selection, producing an overly optimistic result.
The surface in feature space where a classifier changes its predicted class.
A learned vector representation of a token, item, or passage. Similar vectors can reflect learned relationships but do not guarantee factual relevance.
One pass through the training dataset. More epochs are not always better; monitor validation behavior for overfitting.
A measured property or input variable used by a model, such as age, image intensity, or a token representation.
Continuing model training on task- or domain-specific data. Split data carefully and monitor whether the update improves the target task.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall). It is useful when both types of classification error matter.
A model's ability to perform on new examples drawn from the intended population, not merely on examples used to fit or select it.
An optimization procedure that updates parameters in the direction that reduces a differentiable training objective.
A generated statement that is unsupported by evidence, inaccurate, or inconsistent with a source. Retrieval can help but does not itself guarantee correctness.
A precise, testable expectation about an observable outcome under stated conditions. It should connect a research question to measurable evidence.
The overlap between predicted and true regions divided by their union: intersection area / union area. Used for boxes and segmentation masks.
A training hyperparameter controlling the size of optimizer updates. If too high training can be unstable; if too low progress can be slow.
An unnormalized model score. A softmax or sigmoid can transform logits into probabilities; generation temperature rescales logits before sampling.
A mathematical objective measuring mismatch between predictions and target data. Minimizing training loss alone does not guarantee generalization.
A quantitative measure used to evaluate a model or system. Select it to match the task, population, error costs, and research question.
A model learns training-specific details or noise and performs worse on new examples. A large train/validation gap can be a warning.
Among predicted positives, the share that are correct: TP / (TP + FP). Higher precision means fewer false positives.
Among actual positives, the share that are found: TP / (TP + FN). Higher recall means fewer false negatives.
A constraint or penalty that discourages overly complex fits, such as L1 or L2 penalties, dropout, or early stopping.
A significant, evidence-based limitation or unanswered question in prior work that can be investigated with a feasible and ethical study.
A system that retrieves candidate evidence and adds it to a generative model's context. Retrieval relevance and claim support must still be evaluated.
Another name for recall in binary classification: TP / (TP + FN). State the positive class so the result can be interpreted.
A feature attribution based on average marginal contributions across feature coalitions in a specified explanation setup. It explains a model output, not causation.
A data split that approximately preserves class proportions across partitions. It is not a substitute for group-aware or time-aware splitting when observations are dependent.
A decoding parameter that rescales token logits before sampling. Lower values generally concentrate probability; higher values generally spread it.
Examples held out from fitting and model selection for a final evaluation under a preselected protocol. Repeated tuning against it causes leakage.
A unit produced by a text tokenizer. It may be a word, word fragment, punctuation mark, or other unit; a token is not necessarily a word.
A neural-network architecture using attention and feed-forward blocks to build contextual representations of sequence elements.
Sensitivity of a fitted model to changes in its training data. High variance often accompanies overfitting.

formulas.name: Linear prediction
formulas.meaning: A weighted sum of input features plus an intercept predicts a continuous value.

formulas.name: Logistic sigmoid
formulas.meaning: Maps a real-valued score z to a value between 0 and 1, often interpreted as a binary-class probability.

formulas.name: Binary cross-entropy
formulas.meaning: Penalizes probability predictions that assign low probability to the correct binary label. Average over examples for a dataset loss.

formulas.name: Gini impurity
formulas.meaning: Measures class mixing in a node. A node containing one class has Gini impurity zero.

formulas.name: Euclidean distance
formulas.meaning: Straight-line distance between feature vectors. Scale numeric features before distance-based methods when units differ.

formulas.name: Standard score
formulas.meaning: Centers a feature at mean μ and scales by standard deviation σ. Fit μ and σ on training data only.

formulas.name: Min-max scaling
formulas.meaning: Maps training feature values to a bounded interval such as [0, 1]. Values outside the training range can transform outside it.

formulas.name: Precision
formulas.meaning: Of the examples predicted positive, what fraction are truly positive?

formulas.name: Recall / sensitivity
formulas.meaning: Of the truly positive examples, what fraction did the model find?

formulas.name: F1 score
formulas.meaning: The harmonic mean of precision and recall. If both are zero, define the convention used by your metric library.

formulas.name: Intersection over Union
formulas.meaning: Quantifies overlap of predicted and true boxes or masks. It ranges from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (exact overlap).

formulas.name: Paired difference
formulas.meaning: Compute paired differences under matched folds, seeds, or examples. Report the mean difference and uncertainty; repeated folds are not always independent.

formulas.name: Bootstrap interval
formulas.expression: Resample observations with replacement → recompute statistic → take interval quantiles
formulas.meaning: A bootstrap estimates sampling uncertainty for a statistic. Resample at the independent sampling unit and report the interval method and number of resamples.

formulas.name: SHAP additive explanation
formulas.meaning: A baseline prediction plus feature attributions reconstructs a local model output under the explainer's chosen background and output scale.

formulas.name: Attention
formulas.meaning: Queries compare with keys to create weights; those weights combine values. Masks can restrict which positions are visible.

projects.title: Project 1 · Build a fair classifier comparison
projects.goal: Compare a simple baseline with a more flexible classifier using an evaluation protocol that avoids leakage.
projects.materials: Use the supplied four-example classification dataset below. No dataset download or account on another site is needed.
steps: Write the research question and state what outcome is being predicted.
Calculate a majority-class baseline before proposing a complex model.
Specify which examples are used to fit versus evaluate; do not tune on the final test examples.
Report accuracy and the confusion counts; explain what this tiny dataset cannot establish.
List at least three threats to validity before making a claim.
projects.deliverable: A one-page experiment card: question, split, baseline, metric, result, limitation, next experiment.
rubric: A fair baseline using the same data partition.
At least one limitation about sample size or generalization.
No causal claim from predictive association.

projects.title: Project 2 · Explain one prediction responsibly
projects.goal: Compare a global feature ranking with a local explanation and communicate their limits.
projects.materials: Use a small tabular model you create in the Python exercise or a model from Project 1; no external package is required for the planning workbook.
steps: Define the model, target, evaluation population, and baseline output.
Choose one global question and one individual prediction question.
Write what a permutation-based ranking would measure and how correlated features could affect it.
Draft a local explanation in plain language, naming the baseline and explainer assumptions.
Try one plausible counterfactual and discuss whether it is actionable and ethically appropriate.
State explicitly why the explanation does not establish causality or fairness.
projects.deliverable: A two-part explanation card: global behavior, one local case, stability check, cautions.
rubric: Global and local explanation questions are distinguished.
A stability or sensitivity check is proposed.
Attribution is not presented as causal evidence.
The intended user and actionability are stated.

projects.title: Project 3 · Design an evidence-based AI study
projects.goal: Turn a human problem into a feasible, testable research plan.
projects.materials: Begin with a problem you can describe from your own domain knowledge. The provided workbook is sufficient to draft and evaluate a plan.
steps: Describe the people affected and the real decision or outcome at stake.
State what prior evidence would need to be reviewed and what a genuine gap might look like.
Write a focused question with a population, comparison, outcome, and context.
State a falsifiable hypothesis and a result that would disconfirm it.
Specify data access, consent, privacy, group/time split, baseline, metric, and uncertainty.
Identify harms, limitations, and a stopping or escalation rule.
Design one ablation and one robustness check.
projects.deliverable: A reproducible study protocol completed in the Research Studio.
rubric: The question is specific and feasible.
The metric matches the research question.
Ethics, limitations, and a disconfirming result are explicit.

projects.title: Project 4 · Draft a complete research paper
projects.goal: Turn a completed or hypothetical study into a coherent, bounded manuscript.
projects.materials: Use the built-in CRELE abstract outline, section prompts, reproducibility checklist, and submission checklist. Current venue rules should be verified before a real submission.
steps: Write an abstract using Context, Research gap, Approach, Results, Limitations, and Implications.
Explain the question and contribution in the introduction.
Describe data, splits, preprocessing, baselines, metrics, statistics, and compute in the methods.
Organize results around the research question; include uncertainty and failure cases.
Discuss limits, affected groups, ethical risks, and what the evidence does not support.
Use the final checklist to verify figures, references, anonymity rules, and supplemental files.
Choose a venue by scope and official requirements, not an outdated acceptance-rate claim.
projects.deliverable: A structured manuscript draft and submission-readiness checklist.
rubric: Limitations and ethical risks are specific.
The venue's current official instructions are checked for a real submission.

studyPlan.title: Orient
studyPlan.task: Map AI, ML, deep learning, generative models, and agents. Write down one real-world question you care about.

studyPlan.title: Build a baseline
studyPlan.task: Work through Parts II and X. Explain the split, baseline, and metric before looking at a score.

studyPlan.title: Inspect the model
studyPlan.task: Compare an explanation and a failure case. Record what the explanation cannot tell you.

studyPlan.title: Connect representations
studyPlan.task: Choose a vision, language, or generative method and explain its inputs, outputs, and assumptions.

studyPlan.title: Design the study
studyPlan.task: Use the Research Studio to write a question, hypothesis, data plan, baseline, and evaluation.

studyPlan.title: Stress-test the evidence
studyPlan.task: Plan an ablation, uncertainty analysis, robustness test, and ethical review.

studyPlan.title: Write for others
studyPlan.task: Draft the abstract and methodology, run the submission checklist, and list remaining limitations.

paperSections.title: Title
paperSections.prompt: Describe the research problem and contribution clearly without claiming more than the evidence.

paperSections.title: Abstract (CRELE)
paperSections.prompt: Context · Research gap · Approach · Results · Limitations · Implications. Do not invent results.

paperSections.title: Introduction
paperSections.prompt: Motivate the problem, explain the gap, state the research question, summarize contributions, and preview the paper.

paperSections.title: Related work
paperSections.prompt: Group prior work by approach or finding; explain both what is established and what remains unknown.

paperSections.title: Method
paperSections.prompt: Specify data provenance, participants, inclusion criteria, splits, preprocessing, models, baselines, metrics, statistics, and compute.

paperSections.title: Results
paperSections.prompt: Present results tied to the question, uncertainty, appropriate comparisons, ablations, and failure cases.

paperSections.title: Discussion
paperSections.prompt: Interpret findings, avoid unsupported causal claims, explain practical implications, limitations, harms, and next steps.

paperSections.title: Conclusion
paperSections.prompt: Restate the evidence-bounded contribution and the most important limitation.

submissionChecklist: Research question and claims match the actual evidence.
Dataset provenance, permissions, consent, and preprocessing are documented.
Train/validation/test separation and leakage controls are explained.
Baselines, hyperparameters, random seeds, and compute are reported.
Metrics, confidence intervals or statistical tests, and their assumptions are described.
Ablations and relevant subgroup or robustness analyses are included.
Limitations, potential harms, and intended-use boundaries are explicit.
Figures and tables are legible, labeled, and consistent with the text.
Citations, authorship, conflicts, and supplementary materials are checked.
The current official venue template, page limit, anonymity, ethics, and submission rules are verified.
